Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The National Institutes of Health (NIH) awarded a grant of approximately $40 million to a team led by the Yale School of Medicine to develop a CRISPR-based gene-editing platform aimed at treating genetic brain diseases. The research is part of the NIH Common Fund's Somatic Cell Genome Editing program and involves collaboration with the Foundation for Angelman Syndrome Therapeutics and Rush University Medical Center. The project will initially focus on developing therapies for Angelman syndrome and H1-4 (HIST1H1E) syndrome, also known as Rahman syndrome. The grant is structured in two phases: the first phase provides $26.5 million for preclinical studies in animal models and human-brain organoids, while the second, contingent on the success of the first, will provide an additional $13.4 million to fund human clinical trials. <2> On October 3, 2023, Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Intellia Therapeutics announced an expansion of their long-standing research collaboration to develop in vivo CRISPR-based gene editing therapies for neurological and muscular diseases. [1, 2, 7] This strategic partnership aims to overcome a significant hurdle in genetic medicine: delivering therapies to cells beyond the liver. [2, 6] The collaboration combines Regeneron's proprietary antibody-targeted adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors with Intellia's Nme2 CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology. [4, 5, 7] The expanded agreement will initially focus on two non-liver targets. [1, 4, 5] Under the terms, Intellia will lead the design of the editing methodology, while Regeneron will handle the targeted viral vector delivery approach. [4, 5] Each company will have the opportunity to lead the development and commercialization of a product candidate for one target, with the other partner having an option to co-develop and co-commercialize. [1, 6] <3> A research paper published in the journal Nature on September 18, 2023, reported on the first-in-human use of a super-precise CRISPR base editor in a clinical trial in the United States. [1] This milestone marks the U.S. debut of the base editing technique in a clinical setting. The trial, sponsored by Beam Therapeutics, is testing a therapy known as BEAM-201 in patients with relapsed or refractory T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). While the Nature article announced the trial had begun, the company confirmed that the first patient was actually dosed on August 8, 2023. <4> The Congressional Research Service (CRS) published a report, R47683, titled "Gene-Edited Plants: Regulation and Issues for Congress." [3, 4, 5] The document details the U.S. regulatory approach to gene-edited plants under the Coordinated Framework for Regulation of Biotechnology, which coordinates oversight among the USDA, FDA, and EPA. [1, 2] It highlights policy issues for Congress, such as examining whether current regulations and labeling standards, like the National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard, adequately address gene-edited plants and if inter-agency coordination is effective. [1, 2] The report has been updated since its initial release. [6, 7] <5> Excision BioTherapeutics, a clinical-stage biotechnology company, announced that its gene-editing therapy candidate for HIV, EBT-101, received Fast Track Designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). [2] This designation is intended to facilitate development and expedite the review of new drugs that treat serious conditions and address unmet medical needs. [2, 3] EBT-101 is a first-in-class, CRISPR-based gene therapy designed as a potential one-time treatment to functionally cure Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 (HIV-1). [2, 4] The therapy is administered as a single intravenous infusion and utilizes an adeno-associated virus (AAV) to deliver CRISPR-Cas9 and dual guide RNAs. [3, 4] This system targets three distinct sites within the HIV genome, excising large portions of the viral DNA to prevent it from replicating. [3, 4] At the time of the announcement, EBT-101 was being evaluated in an ongoing Phase 1/2 clinical trial to assess its safety and tolerability. [2, 3] <6> On July 17, 2023, Scribe Therapeutics and Sanofi announced an expansion of their existing collaboration to develop in vivo CRISPR-based therapies, with an initial focus on sickle cell disease. [1, 4] Under the agreement, Sanofi gains an exclusive license to Scribe's proprietary CRISPR X-Editing (XE) technologies, which will be combined with Sanofi's non-viral delivery methods. [1, 4] In exchange, Scribe Therapeutics received a $40 million upfront payment and is eligible for over $1.2 billion in potential development and sales milestone payments, in addition to tiered royalties on future net sales. [1, 4, 6] <7> On July 6, 2023, clinical-stage CRISPR genome-editing company Caribou Biosciences announced it had received a $25 million equity investment from Pfizer. [1, 3, 5, 6] The deal, which closed on June 30, 2023, involved Pfizer purchasing 4,690,431 of Caribou's common shares at a price of $5.33 per share. [5, 6, 7] The investment is intended to advance Caribou's immune-cloaked, allogeneic CAR-T cell therapy candidate, CB-011. [1, 2, 3, 4] This therapy is currently being evaluated in the Phase 1 CaMMouflage clinical trial for patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. [1, 2, 3, 4] As part of the investment, Sriram Krishnaswami, a Vice President at Pfizer, joined Caribou's Scientific Advisory Board. [6, 7, 8] <8> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted accelerated approval to Elevidys (delandistrogene moxeparvovec-rokl) on June 22, 2023. [1, 2] This is the first gene therapy approved for the treatment of pediatric patients aged 4 through 5 who have Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and a confirmed mutation in the DMD gene. [1, 2] The approval was granted through the FDA's Accelerated Approval pathway. This tool, named the Integrated Classification Pipeline (ICP), is designed to help identify both intended edits and unintended "bystander" mutations. The system works by decomposing and categorizing mutations generated by CRISPR/Cas9 at genomic target sites. These categorized repair signatures allow for marker-free tracking of specific mutations. The goal of this in-depth analysis of gene editing events is to pave the way for safer and more effective human gene therapies. The research was detailed in the journal Nature Communications on March 23, 2024. <2> In a historic medical first, surgeons at Massachusetts General Hospital successfully transplanted a genetically edited pig kidney into a living human patient on March 16, 2024. [3, 5] The patient, 62-year-old Richard "Rick" Slayman, received the organ during a four-hour procedure. [3, 4] The pig kidney, supplied by eGenesis of Cambridge, MA, was modified using CRISPR-Cas9 technology to enhance its compatibility with the human body. [3, 5] This involved making 69 genomic edits to remove harmful pig genes, add specific human genes, and inactivate porcine endogenous retroviruses to prevent infection. [3] The hospital officially announced the groundbreaking surgery on March 21, 2024. [3, 5, 6] Mr. Slayman, who had a previous human kidney transplant in 2018 that failed, was recovering well after the procedure. The document outlines the necessary information to be included in an Investigational New Drug (IND) application to evaluate the safety and quality of these products. Key areas covered in the guidance include product design, manufacturing and testing, nonclinical safety assessment, and clinical trial design. metadata.original_text: This time series records gene editing data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2024-06-09 to 2024-08-25. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced it will serve as the primary regulator for animals with intentional genomic alterations (IGAs). On May 1, 2024, the agency issued the final Guidance for Industry (GFI) #187A, detailing a risk-based regulatory approach for these genetically engineered animals before they are marketed. This guidance clarifies the FDA's oversight process and aims to make it more efficient and predictable. In conjunction with this, the FDA and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) established a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to clarify each agency's roles and responsibilities, ensuring a seamless regulatory process. While the FDA will lead the oversight, the MOU facilitates enhanced information sharing and consultation with the USDA during the premarket review. This action resolves prior jurisdictional uncertainty between the two departments. <2> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Pfizer's BEQVEZ™ (fidanacogene elaparvovec-dzkt), a one-time gene therapy for the treatment of adults with moderate to severe hemophilia B. [1] This adeno-associated virus vector-based gene therapy is indicated for adults who currently use factor IX (FIX) prophylaxis therapy, have a history of life-threatening hemorrhage, or experience repeated, serious spontaneous bleeding episodes. [2, 3] Patients must also be tested to ensure they do not have neutralizing antibodies to the AAVRh74var capsid. [3] The approval was based on the results of the Phase 3 BENEGENE-2 trial, which demonstrated a reduction in the annualized bleeding rate for patients treated with the gene therapy compared to those on a standard FIX prophylaxis regimen. [2, 7] <3> On April 25, 2024, Ascidian Therapeutics announced it would present preclinical data for its primary RNA exon editing therapy, ACDN-01. The presentation was scheduled for the American Society of Gene & Cell Therapy (ASGCT) annual meeting, which took place in Baltimore, MD, from May 7-11, 2024, with the specific poster session occurring on May 8. The data presented were noted as being supportive of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) prior clearance of the company's Investigational New Drug (IND) application, which permits the start of a Phase 1/2 clinical trial, known as the STELLAR study, for Stargardt disease and other ABCA4 retinopathies. Concurrently with the presentation announcement, Ascidian revealed that the FDA had also granted ACDN-01 a Rare Pediatric Disease Designation. <4> In April 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) issued two draft guidances aimed at improving the safety and quality testing of cell and gene therapy products. The first document, titled "Safety Testing of Human Allogeneic Cells Expanded for Use in Cell-Based Medical Products," outlines recommendations for testing cultured allogeneic cells. The second, "Considerations for the Use of Human-and Animal-Derived Materials in the Manufacture of Cell and Gene Therapy and Tissue-Engineered Medical Products," addresses the safety and quality of raw materials used in manufacturing. These guidances are intended to provide greater regulatory clarity for developers submitting Investigational New Drug Applications (INDs) or Biologics License Applications (BLAs). <5> Researchers at the University of California San Diego developed a new genetic system to analyze and track the mechanisms and inheritance of DNA repair outcomes from CRISPR-based gene editing. This tool, named the Integrated Classification Pipeline (ICP), is designed to help identify both intended edits and unintended "bystander" mutations. The system works by decomposing and categorizing mutations generated by CRISPR/Cas9 at genomic target sites. These categorized repair signatures allow for marker-free tracking of specific mutations. The goal of this in-depth analysis of gene editing events is to pave the way for safer and more effective human gene therapies. The research was detailed in the journal Nature Communications on March 23, 2024. <6> In a historic medical first, surgeons at Massachusetts General Hospital successfully transplanted a genetically edited pig kidney into a living human patient on March 16, 2024. [3, 5] The patient, 62-year-old Richard "Rick" Slayman, received the organ during a four-hour procedure. [3, 4] The pig kidney, supplied by eGenesis of Cambridge, MA, was modified using CRISPR-Cas9 technology to enhance its compatibility with the human body. [3, 5] This involved making 69 genomic edits to remove harmful pig genes, add specific human genes, and inactivate porcine endogenous retroviruses to prevent infection. [3] The hospital officially announced the groundbreaking surgery on March 21, 2024. [3, 5, 6] Mr. Slayman, who had a previous human kidney transplant in 2018 that failed, was recovering well after the procedure. [3, 5] <7> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued its final guidance for the industry concerning foods derived from plants produced using genome editing. This guidance clarifies the agency's consistent risk-based regulatory approach, affirming that these foods must meet the same safety requirements as all other foods. Furthermore, it details two voluntary premarket engagement processes for developers: voluntary premarket consultations and voluntary premarket meetings, allowing firms to engage with the FDA before marketing their products to ensure safety. <8> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a final guidance document titled 'Human Gene Therapy Products Incorporating Human Genome Editing' in January 2024, which was published in the Federal Register on January 30, 2024. This guidance provides recommendations for sponsors and manufacturers developing human gene therapy products that utilize genome editing (GE) of human somatic cells. The document outlines the necessary information to be included in an Investigational New Drug (IND) application to evaluate the safety and quality of these products. Key areas covered in the guidance include product design, manufacturing and testing, nonclinical safety assessment, and clinical trial design. The final version of the guidance clarifies the potential use of the accelerated approval pathway for these therapies, especially for those treating serious or life-threatening diseases with no other treatment options. It finalizes the draft guidance issued in March 2022 and incorporates feedback received from various stakeholders. The FDA also hosted a webinar on February 29, 2024, to discuss key aspects of the final guidance. <9> The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) granted health-focused food and agriculture company Pairwise nine new regulatory exemptions for its gene-edited blackberries and black raspberries. [1, 2] This announcement brings Pairwise's total confirmed trait exemptions for berries to 19 and its overall total to 21. [1, 2] The exemptions cover a range of traits beneficial to both consumers and growers, such as being seedless and thornless, and enabling higher yields. [1, 2] According to the USDA, plants with these types of edits are considered achievable through conventional breeding methods. [2, 3] <10> On January 16, 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expanded the approval of Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), a CRISPR/Cas9 gene-edited cell therapy. [2, 6, 9] This approval allows for the treatment of transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (TDT) in patients aged 12 and older. [8, 9] The decision came less than six weeks after the therapy's historic initial FDA approval on December 8, 2023, for treating sickle cell disease (SCD) in the same age group, making Casgevy the first approved therapy in the U.S. to utilize CRISPR technology. [1, 2, 6]

[1] The company's patent protection efforts were most concentrated in the United States, where it had six publications in the second quarter. [1] Key areas of focus for these patents included cell therapy, hemoglobinopathies, and rare diseases. [1] For rare diseases, nearly 31% of patents were filed and 29% were granted in Q2 2024, while for cell therapy, nearly 5% were filed and 7% were granted during the same period. [1] <2> Immix Biopharma announced on July 8, 2024, that the first patient had been dosed in the Phase 1b/2 NEXICART-2 clinical trial (NCT06097832) in the United States. [1] The trial is evaluating NXC-201, an investigational BCMA-targeted CAR-T cell therapy, for the treatment of relapsed or refractory light chain (AL) amyloidosis. [1, 2] The first patient was treated at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC), the lead site for the study. [2] The NEXICART-2 trial is the only active CAR-T clinical trial in the U.S. for AL amyloidosis patients who have progressed after frontline therapy. [1, 2] It aims to enroll approximately 40 patients with adequate cardiac function who have not previously received a BCMA-targeted therapy. [5, 6] This clearance allows the company to initiate a Phase 1 clinical trial for the natural killer (NK) cell engager therapy. [5] The trial will assess GTB-3650 in patients with relapsed or refractory (r/r) CD33-expressing hematologic malignancies, which include acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). Under the agreement, Ascidian received an upfront payment of $42 million and is eligible for up to $1.8 billion in research, clinical, and commercial milestone payments, in addition to royalties. The partnership will leverage Ascidian's RNA exon editing platform with Roche's central nervous system (CNS) delivery capabilities. Ascidian will lead discovery and some preclinical activities in collaboration with Roche, while Roche will be responsible for further clinical development, manufacturing, and commercialization. This deal marks a significant investment in RNA editing technology and provides Roche with exclusive, target-specific rights to Ascidian's platform. <5> Scientists at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard announced on June 10, 2024, an improved prime editing system capable of inserting or substituting entire genes in human cells at therapeutically relevant efficiencies. This advance, from the lab of David Liu, combines prime editing with newly developed recombinase enzymes to create a system called eePASSIGE, which can perform gene-sized edits more efficiently than previous methods. This development could enable a single gene therapy approach for diseases caused by numerous mutations, such as cystic fibrosis, by inserting a healthy copy of the gene at its native location in the genome. <6> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced it will serve as the primary regulator for animals with intentional genomic alterations (IGAs). This guidance clarifies the FDA's oversight process and aims to make it more efficient and predictable. [3] The approval was based on the results of the Phase 3 BENEGENE-2 trial, which demonstrated a reduction in the annualized bleeding rate for patients treated with the gene therapy compared to those on a standard FIX prophylaxis regimen. [2, 7] <8> On April 25, 2024, Ascidian Therapeutics announced it would present preclinical data for its primary RNA exon editing therapy, ACDN-01. The presentation was scheduled for the American Society of Gene & Cell Therapy (ASGCT) annual meeting, which took place in Baltimore, MD, from May 7-11, 2024, with the specific poster session occurring on May 8. The data presented were noted as being supportive of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) prior clearance of the company's Investigational New Drug (IND) application, which permits the start of a Phase 1/2 clinical trial, known as the STELLAR study, for Stargardt disease and other ABCA4 retinopathies. The first document, titled "Safety Testing of Human Allogeneic Cells Expanded for Use in Cell-Based Medical Products," outlines recommendations for testing cultured allogeneic cells. The second, "Considerations for the Use of Human-and Animal-Derived Materials in the Manufacture of Cell and Gene Therapy and Tissue-Engineered Medical Products," addresses the safety and quality of raw materials used in manufacturing. These guidances are intended to provide greater regulatory clarity for developers submitting Investigational New Drug Applications (INDs) or Biologics License Applications (BLAs). <10> Researchers at the University of California San Diego developed a new genetic system to analyze and track the mechanisms and inheritance of DNA repair outcomes from CRISPR-based gene editing. The system works by decomposing and categorizing mutations generated by CRISPR/Cas9 at genomic target sites. These categorized repair signatures allow for marker-free tracking of specific mutations. The goal of this in-depth analysis of gene editing events is to pave the way for safer and more effective human gene therapies. The research was detailed in the journal Nature Communications on March 23, 2024.

metadata.original_text: This time series records gene editing data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2025-07-06 to 2025-09-21. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On June 3, 2025, a review article titled "Recent developments, challenges and opportunities in genome editing for crop science from a societal perspective" was published in the journal 'Frontiers in Genome Editing'. [8, 9, 13] The article explores the social and regulatory aspects of genome editing concerning food security, discussing both the benefits and potential drawbacks, such as off-target effects. [12] It highlights specific applications of the technology by U.S. companies, referencing Calyxt's generation of a high oleic acid soybean line called Calyno using TALEN technology, and Corteva's development of waxy corn through gene editing. [2, 5] <2> Scientists at Yale University announced the development of sophisticated new mouse models utilizing CRISPR-Cas12a technology, a breakthrough published in the journal Nature Biomedical Engineering. These models, specifically four new Cas12a mouse lines, enable researchers to simultaneously assess multiple complex genetic interactions and their effects on various immunological responses to diseases, including cancer. The new tool enhances disease modeling by allowing scientists to induce and track changes in different immune system cells and fine-tune multiple genes at the same time, overcoming previous limitations of CRISPR-Cas9 technology which could only modify single gene sequences effectively. This advancement facilitates the rapid generation of new models for diseases and treatments. <3> Scientists at Yale University have developed a new CRISPR-based tool using Cas12a that enables the simultaneous assessment of multiple genetic changes. [1, 2, 4] This technology was used to create a series of sophisticated mouse models, allowing researchers to explore complex genetic interactions and their effects on immunological responses to various diseases, including cancer. [2, 4] The new tool facilitates the rapid generation of models for conditions such as genetic diseases in the liver, as well as lung and skin cancer. [2] The findings, co-authored by Sidi Chen, an associate professor of genetics and neurosurgery at Yale School of Medicine, were published in the journal Nature Biomedical Engineering under the title "Cas12a-knock-in mice for multiplexed genome editing, disease modelling and immune-cell engineering". [2, 3, 8] <4> Century Therapeutics has commenced its Phase 1 CALiPSO-1 trial, dosing the first patient in March 2025. [10, 15] The trial is evaluating CNTY-101, an allogeneic, iPSC-derived CAR-iNK cell therapy, for the treatment of various B-cell mediated autoimmune diseases. [5] The study is actively recruiting participants in the United States, with five sites operational and more expected to open in 2025. [8, 10] The trial will enroll patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), lupus nephritis, idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, and diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. [5, 13] The study is sponsored by the Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nürnberg in Germany. [5, 13, 14] Century Therapeutics anticipates expanding the trial to European sites in the second half of 2025. [8] <5> In February 2025, three companies showcased promising advancements in gene-editing therapies for a range of conditions. [1] On February 25, YolTech Therapeutics reported positive results for YOLT-203, a treatment for the rare genetic disorder primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH1). [2, 6] Data from the trial, which began dosing patients in August 2024, showed the therapy was well-tolerated and could reduce harmful urinary oxalate levels by nearly 70%. [2, 9] On February 19, Precision BioSciences announced encouraging initial data for its chronic hepatitis B treatment, PBGENE-HBV, from its ELIMINATE-B trial. [3, 5] The therapy was found to be safe and well-tolerated in the first patient cohort and demonstrated significant antiviral activity. [3] Also on February 19, AccurEdit Therapeutics released data for its hypercholesterolemia therapy, ART002. [4] The results showed that a single dose led to a significant and sustained reduction in LDL-C (bad cholesterol), with the highest reduction approaching 70%. [1, 4] <6> In the first half of 2025, the U.S. government under the Trump administration initiated major funding cuts to scientific and biomedical research, impacting key agencies like the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). On February 7, 2025, the NIH announced a policy to significantly reduce funding to research institutions, which was set to take effect on February 10 but was temporarily halted by lawsuits. Concurrently, the NSF faced significant turmoil, terminating over 1,000 grants, with hundreds targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives in April. By early May, the NSF had stopped payments on all existing grants and ceased awarding new ones. The administration also proposed a budget for fiscal year 2026 that included a nearly $18 billion (about 40%) cut to the NIH. These reductions have been described as a threat to the future of American science, potentially undermining the development of new technologies like CRISPR and causing a "brain drain" as researchers consider leaving U.S. academia. <7> On January 28, 2025, Allogene Therapeutics announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared its Investigational New Drug (IND) application for ALLO-329. [3, 5, 8] ALLO-329 is an investigational, allogeneic, dual-targeting CAR T-cell therapy designed to treat autoimmune diseases by targeting both CD19+ B cells and CD70+ activated T cells. [2, 4] This clearance enables the initiation of the Phase 1 RESOLUTION trial, which is expected to begin in mid-2025. [2, 3] The trial will evaluate the therapy in patients with several autoimmune diseases, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), lupus nephritis (LN), idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, and systemic sclerosis. [1, 4] The therapy incorporates Allogene's Dagger® technology, which aims to reduce or eliminate the need for lymphodepletion prior to treatment. [1, 4] <8> On January 22, 2025, Intellia Therapeutics announced that the first patient had been dosed in its global, pivotal Phase 3 HAELO clinical trial. The study is evaluating NTLA-2002, an investigational in vivo CRISPR/Cas9-based gene-editing therapy, for the treatment of hereditary angioedema (HAE). NTLA-2002 is being developed as a single-dose treatment to prevent life-threatening swelling attacks associated with HAE. The HAELO trial is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study expected to enroll 60 adults with Type I or Type II HAE. Intellia anticipates completing enrollment in the second half of 2025 and submitting a Biologics License Application (BLA) in 2026, with a potential U.S. launch in 2027. <9> Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science announced the development of a new gene-editing technology called minimal versatile genetic perturbation technology (mvGPT). [3, 4] As detailed in a paper published in Nature Communications, the technology is capable of simultaneously and independently editing genes, activating gene expression, and repressing genes within the same cell. [5, 8] In testing on human liver cells, the team successfully corrected a mutation that causes Wilson's disease, while also upregulating a gene associated with type I diabetes treatment and suppressing a gene linked to transthyretin amyloidosis. [4, 5, 7] This multifunctional platform, which combines multiple capabilities into a single, more compact tool, opens new avenues for treating complex genetic diseases. [3, 7]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> REPROCELL USA announced it has submitted a Type II Drug Master File (DMF) to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its StemRNA™ Clinical iPSC Seed Clones. [1, 3] This submission is intended to streamline the regulatory review process for biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies by allowing them to reference REPROCELL's clinical iPSC lines within their own regulatory applications for cell therapy development. [1, 2, 3] The DMF provides detailed documentation on donor eligibility, iPSC derivation methods, and extensive quality control testing, ensuring alignment with standards in the U.S., Europe, and Japan. [1, 3] <2> Synthego, a leading provider of CRISPR solutions, announced the successful acquisition of substantially all of its assets by funds managed by life sciences investment firm Perceptive Advisors. The transaction officially closed on July 18, 2025. Under the new ownership, Synthego will continue its normal operations, and its leadership team, staff, and brand identity will remain in place. The company stated that the partnership strengthens its financial position and provides resources to accelerate innovation and expand its product portfolio. <3> The FDA has revoked Sarepta Therapeutics' platform technology designation for its AAVrh74 viral vector, which is used in gene therapies for various forms of muscular dystrophy. This decision, announced on July 18, 2025, followed the death of a 51-year-old, non-ambulatory patient with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD) who was participating in a Phase 1 clinical trial for the investigational gene therapy, SRP-9004. The patient's death was attributed to acute liver failure. The FDA's announcement also referenced two prior deaths from acute liver failure in patients who had received Elevidys, Sarepta's marketed gene therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), which also utilizes the AAVrh74 vector. In addition to revoking the platform designation, the FDA has placed a clinical hold on all trials for SRP-9004 and another investigational gene therapy, SRP-9003, and requested that Sarepta voluntarily halt all shipments of Elevidys. <4> Rocket Pharmaceuticals announced that its investigational adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based gene therapy, RP-A601, received Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy (RMAT) designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This therapy is being developed to treat plakophilin-2 related arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (PKP2-ACM), a life-threatening heart condition that can cause ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. The RMAT designation, which is intended to expedite the development and review of promising therapies, was granted based on positive safety and efficacy data from the Phase 1 clinical trial of RP-A601. This is the fifth RMAT designation in the company's history. <5> Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical Inc. announced it received a Complete Response Letter (CRL) from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its Biologics License Application (BLA) for UX111 (also known as ABO-102). This treatment is an adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapy for patients with Sanfilippo syndrome type A, or mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIA (MPS IIIA). The CRL requested additional information and improvements related to Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC) and also cited observations from recent inspections of the manufacturing facilities. Ultragenyx stated its belief that the cited observations are resolvable, relate to facilities and processes rather than product quality, and that many have already been addressed. While the FDA's clinical review acknowledged that the neurodevelopmental outcome data is robust, the CRL will delay the potential approval of UX111 to 2026. Ultragenyx plans to work with the FDA to resolve the issues and resubmit the BLA, which would be followed by an anticipated six-month review period. <6> An American study published in Nature Communications details a CRISPR-Cas9-based system that enables both random access and similarity search within DNA-based data storage, representing a significant advancement in molecular data technologies. [1] The research, authored by Carina Imburgia, Lee Organick, and others from the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science and Engineering and Microsoft Research, introduces a one-pot, multiplexed random access method. This approach uses a CRISPR-Cas9 addressing system to selectively cleave specific data files from a large pool of DNA sequences, which are then sequenced using nanopore technology. The study also presents a molecular similarity-search method that combines machine learning with Cas9-based retrieval, allowing for the identification of semantically related data. This platform is highlighted for its potential to provide scalable, rapid, and energy-efficient access to molecular data. [1] <7> Atsena Therapeutics announced it reached an agreement with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to expand its ongoing Phase 1/2 LIGHTHOUSE study for ATSN-201 into a pivotal Phase 1/2/3 trial. [4, 6] ATSN-201 is an investigational gene therapy for the treatment of X-linked retinoschisis (XLRS). [2] This expansion allows the trial to serve as a basis for a future Biologics License Application (BLA) submission, which is anticipated in early 2028. [4, 6] The agreement followed a Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy (RMAT) meeting and is expected to accelerate the clinical development of ATSN-201 by at least 1.5 years compared to conducting a separate Phase 3 trial. [2, 4] Enrollment for the pivotal cohort is planned to start in the first quarter of 2026. [1, 4] <8> On July 8, 2025, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI) and the Innovative Genomics Institute (IGI) announced that CZI awarded a $20 million grant to the IGI to create the Center for Pediatric CRISPR Cures. [2, 4, 7] This new center is a collaborative effort between the University of California, Berkeley, which will handle CRISPR cure design and testing, and the University of California, San Francisco, which will manage clinical treatment. [2, 5, 7] The center's goal is to develop personalized, on-demand CRISPR-based therapies for children with severe rare genetic diseases, initially focusing on metabolic and immune system disorders. [3, 5, 6] The initiative aims to build upon the recent success of a personalized CRISPR treatment for an infant, with an initial goal of treating eight patients and establishing a standardized process to make these cures more accessible. [1, 5, 6] <9> Eli Lilly and Company successfully completed its acquisition of Verve Therapeutics on July 25, 2025. [3, 5, 8] Verve is a clinical-stage company specializing in the development of in vivo gene editing therapies for cardiovascular disease. [1, 3] The acquisition followed the expiration of a tender offer on July 23, 2025, in which approximately 55.7% of Verve's outstanding shares were tendered. [4, 6, 7] The definitive agreement for the acquisition was first announced on June 17, 2025. [1, 13] Under the terms of the deal, Lilly acquired Verve for $10.50 per share in cash, plus one non-tradable contingent value right (CVR) per share, entitling the holder to a potential additional payment of up to $3.00. [4, 9] The total potential value of the transaction is approximately $1.3 billion. [1, 10, 11] This acquisition is intended to advance the development of one-time gene editing treatments for patients with high cardiovascular risk. [12, 14] <10> On June 3, 2025, a review article titled "Recent developments, challenges and opportunities in genome editing for crop science from a societal perspective" was published in the journal 'Frontiers in Genome Editing'. [8, 9, 13] The article explores the social and regulatory aspects of genome editing concerning food security, discussing both the benefits and potential drawbacks, such as off-target effects. [12] It highlights specific applications of the technology by U.S. companies, referencing Calyxt's generation of a high oleic acid soybean line called Calyno using TALEN technology, and Corteva's development of waxy corn through gene editing. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> FDA officials Vinay Prasad, M.D., and Martin Makary, M.D., have unveiled a novel regulatory program dubbed the 'plausible mechanism pathway.' Detailed in a New England Journal of Medicine article, this new pathway is designed to accelerate the development and regulatory approval of bespoke, customized gene editing therapies. The initiative is specifically tailored to offer a new route to market for personalized treatments, prioritizing individual patients suffering from rare diseases, particularly those that are fatal or involve severe childhood disabilities, while remaining available for common diseases as well. <2> Metagenomi announced a strategic restructuring that includes a 25% workforce reduction and a change in leadership, with new CEO Jian Irish replacing founder Brian Thomas. This reshuffle aims to extend the company's cash runway to the fourth quarter of 2027, directing funds toward advancing its lead in vivo gene-editing candidate, MGX-001, into clinical testing as a one-time treatment for hemophilia A. <3> ERS Genomics and Jupiter, Florida-based Dyadic Applied BioSolutions have signed a non-exclusive license agreement granting Dyadic access to ERS's foundational CRISPR/Cas9 patent portfolio. This agreement enables Dyadic to accelerate microbial strain engineering and pathway optimization across its proprietary bioproduction platforms. <4> On November 8, 2025, Cleveland Clinic presented Phase 1 clinical trial data at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2025, demonstrating that CRISPR Therapeutics' experimental CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing therapy, CTX310, safely reduced LDL cholesterol by 50% and triglycerides by approximately 55%. The first-in-human trial reported no serious safety events related to the treatment. <5> Intellia Therapeutics announced the death of a hospitalized patient who experienced severe liver toxicity, marked by grade 4 liver enzymes and increased total bilirubin, after receiving the investigational CRISPR-based gene therapy nex-z. Following the disclosure of this safety signal, the FDA placed the company's Phase 3 clinical trials on hold. <6> Azalea Therapeutics, an in vivo gene editing biotechnology company spun out of Nobel laureate Jennifer Doudna's laboratory at UC Berkeley, has officially launched. The company debuted with $82 million in combined seed and Series A financing to advance its proprietary Enveloped Delivery Vehicle (EDV) technology, which selectively targets cells to deliver transient CRISPR-Cas9 cargo for programmable genome editing directly inside the patient. <7> The FDA placed a clinical hold on Intellia Therapeutics' Phase 3 MAGNITUDE and MAGNITUDE-2 clinical trials for its in vivo CRISPR-based gene editing therapy, nex-z, after a patient developed life-threatening liver toxicity. The holds were simultaneously initiated on October 29, 2025. <8> Scientists at The University of Texas at Austin have announced the development of a revolutionary gene-editing method utilizing bacterial retrons. This new approach allows for the efficient replacement of large defective DNA regions and enables the simultaneous correction of multiple disease-causing mutations within a single stretch of DNA. <9> On October 14, 2025, Krystal Biotech announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted a platform technology designation to its genetically modified, non-replicating herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) viral vector. This proprietary viral vector is utilized in KB801, the company's investigational redosable eye drop gene therapy currently being evaluated in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial for the treatment of neurotrophic keratitis (NK). <10> Kite, a Gilead Company, announced the acquisition of Interius BioTherapeutics, a privately held biotechnology company focused on developing in vivo CAR gene therapies, for $350 million. The acquisition will integrate Interius into Gilead's cell therapy-focused Kite subsidiary, providing an innovative in vivo platform designed to generate CAR T-cells directly within a patient's body.
